questions.question: A chemist fills a beaker with pure water and measures its pH: 7, the middle of the scale, neither acid nor base. Even pure water is not all whole molecules, for a tiny share of them are always split into charged pieces called ions. What makes the water neutral?
questions.answer: Just as many hydrogen as hydroxide ions
choices: Just as many hydrogen as hydroxide ions
A few more hydrogen ions than hydroxide ions
A few more hydroxide ions than hydrogen ions
So few ions that neither kind can count
questions.context: An acid adds hydrogen ions to water and a base adds hydroxide ions, so a few extra of either kind would tip the water toward acid or base. Pure water holds a few of both, exactly balanced, and that balance, not a lack of ions, is what neutral means.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.6D) compares acids and bases by their pH relative to water, with pure water as the neutral 7 between them, and teaches acids as givers of hydrogen ions and bases of hydroxide ions.

questions.question: Rain made acid by the fumes of coal-burning power stations falls on a lake year after year, and the lake water slips from pH 7 to pH 5. At pH 5, most fish eggs can no longer hatch. How much more acidic has the lake become?
choices: 100 times as acidic
10 times as acidic
Twice as acidic
1,000 times as acidic
questions.context: Each step down the pH scale means ten times as many hydrogen ions, so the two steps from 7 to 5 mean ten times ten, a hundredfold. Counting the numbers 7, 6 and 5 as three steps gives a thousand, and reading the gap of two as twice misses the tens altogether.
questions.grade_note: The 8th-grade map line's 'the farther from 7, the stronger' is taught with the tenfold step, and acid rain is the grade's example of an acid in nature.

questions.question: A nurse draws a sample of blood from a healthy man's arm for testing. His body keeps his blood within a very narrow band of pH, and he falls dangerously ill if it strays far outside it. Where on the pH scale is healthy blood held?
choices: Just above 7, slightly basic
Just below 7, slightly acidic
Exactly at 7, perfectly neutral
Near 10, as basic as soapy water
questions.context: Healthy blood stays between pH 7.35 and 7.45, a touch on the basic side of neutral. If it falls below 7.35 doctors call it acidosis, and below about 7.2 the danger to life climbs steeply. Soapy water, at about 9 to 10, is far more basic.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons place body fluids on the pH scale beside lab and household ones; blood, just above 7, is the standard body example of a base.

questions.question: Two bottles stand on a laboratory shelf. One holds battery acid, the sulfuric acid inside a car battery, at a pH below 1. The other holds lye, the sodium hydroxide in drain cleaners, at a pH of 14. Which of them can badly burn skin?
questions.answer: Both, as each lies far from 7
choices: Both, as each lies far from 7
Only the battery acid, an acid
Only the lye, with the higher number
Neither, unless the two are mixed
questions.context: The farther a liquid sits from 7, on either side, the stronger it is, and both ends of the scale burn. Lye, a strong base, eats deep into skin, and some strong bases do more harm than acids, though many people think only acids are dangerous. Drain cleaners use it because it dissolves the fat and hair that block pipes.
questions.grade_note: The 8th-grade map line teaches 'the farther from 7, the stronger', with battery acid and strong household bases as its examples.

questions.question: Litmus is a dye made from lichens, used to sort acids from bases since about 1300. A chemist touches one strip of red litmus paper to soapy water and another to household ammonia. Both strips turn blue. What do the two blue strips show?
questions.answer: Both are bases, but not which is stronger
choices: Both are bases, but not which is stronger
Both are bases, and of equal strength
Both are neutral, neither acid nor base
Both are acids, but not which is stronger
questions.context: Red litmus turns blue in a base and blue litmus turns red in an acid, and that is all litmus says: one colour or the other, with no number. Soapy water sits near pH 9 or 10 and household ammonia near 11.5, far more basic, yet both strips turn the same blue. Telling them apart takes pH paper with many colours, or a pH meter.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade teaches indicators, litmus above all, as the way to show whether a substance is an acid or a base (curriculum line G8.P4).

questions.question: A student boils chopped red cabbage in water and strains off the purple juice, an indicator she has made herself. A few drops of it turn red in an acid and green in soapy water. What makes the juice change colour?
questions.answer: Its pigment gains or loses hydrogen ions
choices: Its pigment gains or loses hydrogen ions
Its pigment is bleached by the acid or base
Its pigment mixes with the sample's own colour
Its pigment breaks apart into single atoms
questions.context: The purple comes from a pigment called anthocyanin. An acid loads its molecules with hydrogen ions and a base strips them away, and each change reshapes the molecule and gives it a new colour: red, purple, blue, green, and yellow in the strongest bases. The change runs both ways, so nothing is bleached away, and every colour is the pigment's own.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade classes make a red cabbage indicator as their test-it-yourself, and the grade's acids unit explains acids and bases by hydrogen ions.

questions.question: Heartburn is the burning felt behind the breastbone when acid from the stomach washes back up into the gullet. A man with heartburn chews an antacid tablet, a base that dissolves in his stomach juice. As the tablet works, what happens to the pH in his stomach?
choices: It rises toward 7
It falls toward 0
It rises far past 7
It stays just the same
questions.context: The base in the tablet reacts with some of the stomach's acid and uses it up, so fewer hydrogen ions are left and the pH climbs. A typical antacid lifts the stomach from between 1.5 and 3.5 to about 4 or 5: toward neutral, but not all the way, and never over into the bases.
questions.grade_note: The 8th-grade map line ends with an acid and a base neutralising each other; the antacid is the standard example of the pH moving toward 7.

questions.question: The same acid rain falls for years on two lakes. One lies in a basin of limestone, a rock made mostly of calcium carbonate. The other lies on granite, a hard rock of quartz and feldspar. Which lake stays closer to neutral?
questions.answer: The limestone lake, whose rock neutralises acid
choices: The limestone lake, whose rock neutralises acid
The granite lake, whose rock neutralises acid
The granite lake, whose hard rock resists acid
Both alike, since the very same rain falls on each
questions.context: Calcium carbonate acts as a base, and many antacid tablets are made of it, so as acid water soaks through limestone the rock dissolves a little and uses the acid up. Granite resists acid, which is why it lasts in buildings, but a rock that resists acid does nothing to the acid, so lakes on granite and similar rocks grow more acidic than lakes on limestone.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade applies neutralising to nature as well as the body: acid rain is the grade's example of an acid, and limestone's power to neutralise it is the rock example.

questions.question: Søren Sørensen ran the chemistry department of the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen, where he studied how acidity changes proteins. In 1909 he proposed a scale he called pH. What did his scale give chemists?
questions.answer: One short number for how acidic a sample is
choices: One short number for how acidic a sample is
The first way to tell acids from bases
The first idea that acids give hydrogen ions
Numbers that rise as acids grow stronger
questions.context: Chemists could already tell acids from bases with litmus, used since about 1300, and Svante Arrhenius had argued in 1884 that acids give water extra hydrogen ions. What they lacked was a simple, agreed way to write how many, amounts as tiny as 0.0000001 for pure water. Sørensen turned each into a short number: 7 for pure water, lower for acids and higher for bases.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade learns the pH scale itself, and its maker, Sørensen in 1909, is the how-we-know story behind it (curriculum line G8.P4).

questions.question: The juice inside a person's stomach is hydrochloric acid at about pH 2, and it bathes the stomach wall from the inside. Yet the wall is not eaten away. What protects it?
questions.answer: A layer of mucus kept near neutral by a base
choices: A layer of mucus kept near neutral by a base
A tough outer skin like the skin of the hand
An acid too weak to harm living cells
Cells made of something acid cannot harm
questions.context: Cells in the stomach lining coat it with thick mucus and give off bicarbonate, a base, into that layer. The base neutralises the acid that reaches it, so the pH climbs from about 2 in the middle of the stomach to nearly 7 against the wall. The lining of the gullet makes no such base, which is why acid splashing up into it burns as heartburn.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade's acids unit uses stomach acid, near pH 2, as its body example of an acid, and neutralising by a base is the unit's last idea.
